head:
Health · Mobility

Getting up from the floor: what does this movement say about your health?

Sit on the floor, then get back up without using your hands. Brazilian doctors turned this movement into a test scored out of 10 and found that the lowest scores go with more deaths in the following years. This article follows the reasoning step by step: what is established, what is not, and what you can do with it in practice.

The question

Can a movement that takes under two minutes and needs no equipment really say something about your future health? Put like that, it sounds like a clickbait headline. When you read that a one-minute test "predicts death", the right reaction is suspicion.

Yet the subject deserves a close look, for a simple reason. Getting up from the floor is a movement we lose without deciding to. At 20, you sit on the floor without thinking about it. Then you reach for a sofa, a chair. One day the movement takes effort, and nobody knows since when. If this movement sums up the state of the body well, we have a free benchmark. If it sums up nothing, we waste time and worry for no reason.

The question

Does getting up from the floor without help measure anything real about your future health?

And if so, is it just a thermometer, or a movement you can work on to change what comes next?

To answer, we start from what is observed in large groups, then narrow down: what the figures show, what explains them, what could distort them, and what is known about the possibility of acting.

What is at stake for you

Your independence. Getting up from the floor is what separates an ordinary fall from a problem. The World Health Organization estimates about 842,000 deaths from falls worldwide in 2023, of which about 71% were in people aged 60 and over.10 In France, in 2024, Santé publique France counts, among people aged 65 and over, 174,824 hospitalisations and 20,148 deaths linked to a fall, with rates up by 20.5% and 18% compared with 2019.11 Behind these figures lies what the WHO describes: an injury can lead to a loss of confidence, less activity, and a growing cycle of frailty.10

Your healthy lifespan. There is a lot of talk about cardiorespiratory fitness for longevity. Claudio Gil Araújo, the doctor behind the test, answers that other qualities matter too: strength, flexibility, balance.4,15 If that is true, measuring these qualities with a movement that needs no equipment changes how you can monitor yourself.

Your training. A test is useful if it tells you what to work on. This one is scored point by point: each support used (a hand, a knee, a forearm) removes one point.4 So you can see where you lose points and track progress from one year to the next.

Your peace of mind. A message such as "this test predicts your death" needlessly worries someone who fails it on a tired day, and needlessly reassures someone who scores 10 and neglects everything else. Knowing what these studies show, and what they do not show, protects you from both mistakes.

If the link is real, ignoring it deprives you of a benchmark. If it is overestimated, believing in it puts you under pressure for nothing.
rest:
The demonstration, in six steps

We go from the broadest observation to the most precise questions.

  1. In a large group of adults, is the score linked to survival?
  2. Over a longer period and by cause of death, does the link hold?
  3. Compared with other physical measures, is this an exception or the rule?
  4. In real life, what happens when you cannot get up?
  5. Facing objections, what could distort this link?
  6. Facing action, can the score be changed, and does that change anything?
Step 1 of 6 · A large group of adults

Among adults aged 51 to 80, a low score goes with more deaths

The first study dates from 2012. Araújo's team, in its exercise medicine clinic in Rio de Janeiro, tested 2,002 adults aged 51 to 80, then followed them until their death or until 31 October 2011. The median follow-up was 6.3 years, and 159 people died, or 7.9%.1,2

The test works like this: the participant sits down on the floor then gets back up using as few supports as possible, "without worrying about speed". It takes less than two minutes.1 Out of 10 points, 5 are for sitting down and 5 for getting up, and each support removes one point.1,4 The researchers split the scores into four groups and compared death rates with the best group (8 to 10), at equal age, sex and body mass index (BMI).2

The lower the score, the higher the observed risk of death

Bars: risk ratio. Line with dots: 95% confidence interval (CI), that is, the zone where the true value most likely lies. Dotted line: value 1, the risk of the reference group. The interval for the lowest group is wide (3.1 to 9.5): the study counts only 159 deaths in all. Source: Araújo et al., European Journal of Preventive Cardiology, 2012, via the American College of Cardiology summary.2

What this means

A ratio of 5.44 does not mean a 544% chance of dying. It compares death rates: over the follow-up period, the group that scored 0 to 3 died about 5 times more often than the one that scored 8 to 10. The researchers add that each extra point of score goes with 21% lower mortality.1,2 For you: the slope is continuous. There is no magic threshold; every support counts.

This is a first finding, from a single study and a single 6-year follow-up. We still need to see whether it holds over a longer period and whether it depends on the cause of death.

Step 2 of 6 · Longer, by cause of death

Twelve years later, the same finding, including for the heart

In 2025, the same team published a second study of 4,282 adults aged 46 to 75 (mean age 59, 32% women), tested in a private clinic by doctors trained in the protocol. The follow-up lasts 12.3 years on average. 665 participants, or 15.5%, died.4,5 This time, the scores are split into five groups, from the perfect score of 10 to the 0 to 4 group.5

Over twelve years, the share of deaths rises as the score falls

Share of participants who died during follow-up (12.3 years on average), all causes, raw values without adjustment. The numbers per group are not given in the summaries. The assignment of three of the values to the intermediate groups follows TCTMD; Pharmazeutische Zeitung and zm-online give the same values without specifying which group each belongs to. Source: Araújo et al., European Journal of Preventive Cardiology, 2025, via TCTMD, Pharmazeutische Zeitung and zm-online.4,5,6

Two other results complete this chart. After adjustment for age, sex, BMI and clinical parameters, the 0 to 4 group had a 3.84 times higher risk of dying of natural causes, and a 6.05 times higher risk of dying of a cardiovascular cause, compared with the group scoring 10.5 And at 10 years, 97% of participants with a score of 10 are still alive, compared with 88% of those scoring 8 and 73% of those scoring 0 to 4.4

What this means

The lowest group brings together people who needed substantial help or were very unsteady when sitting down or getting up.4 Even among them, nearly three in four were alive ten years later: the score is not an individual verdict. But the cardiovascular figure (6 times higher) shows that the link also appears for deaths related to the heart and blood vessels, not only for overall mortality. For you: a poor score is not only a matter of joints.

Two studies, one direction. But they come from the same team and the same clinic. To know whether this is a peculiarity of this test, we need to look at what other measures give, made by other researchers.

Step 3 of 6 · Other physical measures

This is not specific to this test: strength and speed say the same thing

The question is this: if the movement of getting up from the floor is only a reflection of general fitness, other measures of physical capability should also go with lifespan. A systematic review published in the BMJ in 2010 (Cooper, Kuh and Hardy) pooled 28 studies conducted in the general population, that is, in people living at home rather than hospitalised patients. They measured hand strength (grip), walking speed, the time to get up from a chair and standing balance. For each measure, the researchers compare the weakest quarter with the strongest quarter.7

Hand strength, chair and walking: the weakest quarter dies more often

Risk ratios adjusted for age, sex and height or weight, weakest quarter versus strongest quarter. The grey dot is a subgroup of studies. The studies differ from one measure to another: we cannot conclude that walking "predicts" better than grip. The walking, chair and balance studies all involve people with a mean age above 61, most of them above 70. Source: Cooper, Kuh and Hardy, BMJ, 2010.7

What this means

Three measures made by other teams, with other movements, converge: the weakest people die more often. Getting up from the floor is therefore not an isolated curiosity. One detail matters for you: grip was also studied in younger groups, where the link is still present (1.43), slightly weaker. For the floor movement, we do not have this data below the age of 46.

The authors of the review also note that results vary a great deal from one study to another for grip and the chair, that estimates are not always adjusted for activity level or social situation, and that there is no clear threshold that would allow a screening limit to be set.7 We come back to this in step 5.

The statistical link is therefore found elsewhere. A more concrete question now arises: why might being unable to get up matter in real life?

Step 4 of 6 · The mechanism in real life

Being unable to get up turns a fall into a serious problem

The test movement brings together several qualities at once. Araújo cites muscular strength, flexibility, the ratio between power and body weight, and coordination.3 In the mainstream press, he also describes the test as a reflection of strength, balance, flexibility and body composition, and specifies that it is not perfect.15 The score does not say which one is lacking: weak thighs, stiff hips or ankles, hesitant balance, weight that makes the movement more costly. It does say, however, that somewhere the margin has shrunk.

These qualities are not abstract. The most concrete evidence comes from a British study of very old people, published in the BMJ in 2008. It followed for one year 110 people over 90 (aged 91 to 105, median age 94) living in Cambridge, with fall diaries and visits.8

Among people over 90, most of those who fall cannot get up on their own

Number of people (1 square = 1 person, common scale). Cambridge cohort, 110 participants aged 91 to 105: small sample, very old population, results not to be transposed as they are to adults of 50 or 60. Source: prospective cohort study, BMJ, 2008.8

Of the 66 people who fell, 53 (80%) could not get up without help after at least one fall. 82% of falls happened while the person was alone.8 20 people, or 30% of those who fell, stayed on the floor for an hour or more at least once. Among them, 12 (60%) were hospitalised because of that fall, odds about 4 times higher after adjustment (odds ratio of 4.0, interval 1.3 to 12.3, very wide given the small numbers).8 The authors conclude that staying on the floor for a long time is more common than was thought among the oldest people, that the consequences are serious, and that people need to be trained to get up from the floor.8

What this means

The test is not an exercise for its own sake: it reproduces, in controlled conditions, a real situation in which you find yourself on the ground. Getting up alone, without support, then becomes a safety skill. This gives a plausible meaning to the observed link: a person who loses this ability is exposed to heavier consequences in the event of a fall. Be careful, however: this study does not measure the score on the floor test, and it does not concern mortality. It is a possible mechanism, not a demonstration of the link with deaths.

The picture is coherent: a statistical link, found with other measures, with a plausible mechanism. This is the moment to look for what could distort all of this.

Step 5 of 6 · The objections

What can distort the link, and what that changes

A statistical link is not a cause. Here are the most serious objections, and what the sources allow us to answer.

Illness may explain everything

A chronic illness can at once weaken the legs, damage balance and shorten life. In that case, the test would only be picking out people who are already ill, and getting up poorly would not be the cause of anything. This is called reverse causation. In the 2012 study, the adjustment covers only age, sex and BMI.1,2 In the 2025 one, one summary mentions "clinical parameters" without detailing them, another reports no adjustment variable.4,5 Smoking, activity level or existing illnesses are not mentioned in the summaries I was able to read. The BMJ review also cites reverse causation and the fact that activity level and social situation are not always taken into account.7

What was measured comes from a single place

Both studies come from the same team, from the same private centre in Rio de Janeiro, with participants who came for an exercise medicine check-up.4 They are not necessarily representative of the population. I did not find, in the open sources, a mortality study on this test carried out by another team. That is what makes step 3 important: it shows a convergence with neighbouring measures, not a replication of the test itself.

The numbers are small in places

In 2012 there were 159 deaths, of which only two among the participants who scored 10 out of 10.3 Hence the wide intervals, such as 3.1 to 9.5 for the lowest group. The figure of 5.44 is an estimate, not an exact measurement.

A group is not you

Risk ratios compare groups. In the lowest group of 2025, 73% of people were alive at 10 years.4 None of these studies makes it possible to say what will happen to a given person. The authors themselves present the test as a screening tool used in a supervised setting, and Araújo says he does not see it as something people should practise alone.4

Age and sex

The first study had 68% men, the second 32% women.2,4 A cardiologist outside the study, Prashant Rao, thinks there is no real difference between the sexes, because men have more strength and women more flexibility, which evens out the total score. That is his interpretation, reported by TCTMD, not a quantified result.4 As for age, no mortality data go below 46.5

What this means

None of these objections makes the link disappear, but they change its scope. The test is a marker: a low score signals a higher risk in a group, for reasons that may be illness as much as weakness. For anyone who only wants to take stock, this is not a problem. For anyone who wants to know whether improving the score changes anything, the question remains entirely open. That is the subject of the last step.

If the test marks a risk, can we act on it? This last step is the most precise, and the least documented.

Step 6 of 6 · Taking action

Strength can be improved and falls reduced; for lifespan, it is open

Let us separate three questions, because their levels of evidence are not the same.

Can you gain strength? Yes, this is very well established. A Cochrane review on progressive strength training in older people brings together 121 randomised trials and 6,700 participants. It concludes there is a large effect on muscular strength (73 trials, standardised effect of 0.84) and a moderate to large effect on chair rise time (11 trials, 384 participants). Serious adverse events are rare and none was judged directly related to the programme.12 For you: the qualities the test calls on can be trained.

Can you reduce falls? Yes, with a high level of evidence. The Cochrane review on exercise to prevent falls (abridged version in the British Journal of Sports Medicine) pools 59 trials and 12,981 participants living at home. Exercise programmes reduce the rate of falls by about 23% (rate ratio 0.77).9,10

Balance and strengthening programmes reduce the number of falls

Fall rate ratio, exercise programme versus no programme, with 95% confidence interval. In the accent colour: the interval does not touch 1. In grey: the interval contains 1, and these types of exercise rest on very few trials (2 and 1), so we cannot conclude that they do not work. Strength training alone has no separate estimate in the text and the authors say they are uncertain about its effect. Source: Sherrington et al., Cochrane review (abridged version), British Journal of Sports Medicine.9

What this means

Programmes that combine balance and functional exercises reduce falls by about a quarter, with a high level of evidence. Programmes that add strengthening go slightly further (0.66), with a moderate level of evidence, but the confidence intervals of the two groups overlap: we cannot say that one does better than the other. For you: what protects against falls is precisely the qualities the test calls on. But these trials do not go through the score on the floor test. They measure falls, not deaths.

Can you live longer by training? It is plausible, but not demonstrated by these studies. A meta-analysis of 16 cohort studies published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine in 2022 finds that people who do strength training have a 15% lower risk of death from all causes (7 of these studies cover this outcome); the lowest risk is reached at about 40 minutes per week. But these are observations, with possible publication bias, mostly from the United States.13 People who train are also often more attentive to their health in general. For the test itself, TCTMD reports that the team's upcoming work aims to determine whether improving the score through exercise brings a survival advantage. I did not find a study that has already done so.4 The authors of the BMJ review also call for randomised trials to find out whether improving physical capability reduces mortality.7

What this means

We know how to train strength, we know how to reduce falls. We do not yet know whether raising your score on the floor test lengthens life. The demonstrated benefits (strength, fewer falls, hence more independence) are already worth the effort, without waiting for this evidence.

The answer to the question

Back to the starting question: does getting up from the floor without help measure anything real about your future health?

What is solid. In two studies by the same team, covering 2,002 then 4,282 adults aged 46 to 80, a low score goes with more deaths, including cardiovascular ones, and the relationship is graded. The same type of link is found, by other teams, with hand grip, chair rise and walking speed. And we know that working on balance and strength reduces falls.

What is probable. The score sums up several physical qualities that are useful in real life, and these matter most when you fall: staying on the floor for a long time has, among people over 90, serious consequences. The test is therefore a reasonable benchmark of a physical margin, useful for deciding what to work on.

What is not established. That getting up poorly is a cause of death rather than the sign of an illness or a lifestyle. That improving the score lengthens life. That the test applies as it stands under 46. That it is reliable as a self-test, without supervision.

The honest answer is therefore this: it is a serious thermometer, not a crystal ball, and it is not yet a demonstrated lever for lifespan. On the other hand, the qualities it measures can be trained, and that work has demonstrated benefits.

What to put in place

Here is how to use this test and the page, in measured doses and without promising what the studies do not demonstrate.

  1. Do the test in good conditions.On a soft surface, with a stable piece of furniture within reach, a person nearby to note the score, without rushing (the study's instruction is not to worry about speed).1 If you have joint pain, an injury or a health problem, ask a doctor first.15
  2. Note the score and where you lose points.Hand, knee, forearm, side of the leg, loss of balance: each support counts one point, a loss of balance half a point.4,5 Where you help yourself tells you whether to work more on thigh strength, hip and ankle mobility, or balance (the editorial team's reading, not a study result).
  3. Place yourself relative to the threshold of 8.In the 2025 study, scores below 8 were associated with higher mortality than scores of 8 or more.4 This is not a diagnosis. A very low score, or being unable to get up, justifies talking to a doctor; a score of 8 or more does not exempt you from continuing to train.
  4. Work on strength and balance every week.The WHO guidelines call for strength training activities at least two days a week; for people aged 65 and over, activities combining balance, coordination and strengthening at least three days a week, to prevent falls.14 It is these combined programmes that gave the largest drop in falls in the trials.9 In cohorts, the benefit of strength training was already clear at around 30 to 60 minutes per week.13
  5. Train the movement itself, gently.Sit on the floor and get back up at your own pace, next to a support, between strength sessions. No study validates this movement as a programme for raising the score: it is common sense resting on the fact that the qualities it calls on can be trained.12
  6. Retest at regular intervals.Every three to six months, in the same conditions (same surface, same time, same clothing), then once a year when you are stable. This interval is advice from the editorial team, not a study result. A score that drops from one year to the next, or a recent fall, deserves to be discussed with your doctor.
What these studies do not say
  • The link between score and death is observational: it does not prove that getting up better makes you live longer.
  • The two studies on the test come from the same team and the same private clinic. No independent replication found.
  • Participants were aged between 46 and 80. Nothing on mortality below or above.
  • No study read shows that the floor test score predicts falls: the link with falls comes from other trials.

Frequently asked questions

If I cannot do it without my hands, will I die earlier?

Nothing makes it possible to say so for a given person. The figures compare groups. In the lowest group of the 2025 study, 73% of participants were alive at 10 years.4 A low score is a signal to take stock, not an individual prediction.

If my score goes up, does my risk go down?

It is plausible, but not demonstrated. What is demonstrated: balance and strengthening exercise reduces falls, with a high level of evidence.9

Is this test better than hand grip or walking speed?

The open sources do not allow us to say. The figures in step 3 come from different studies and I did not find a study that directly compares these measures with the floor test.

Do these results apply to women and to people under 46?

For women, the 2025 study included 32% and an outside commentator judges that there is no real difference between the sexes, with no detailed figures in the open sources.4 For people under 46, none of these studies provides mortality data.5
